title: Unequal Footprints: Comparing Catch Composition and Ecological Indicators Across Small‐Scale Fishery Métiers
content:
ABSTRACT

Small-scale fisheries (SSF) play an important role in coastal Mediterranean communities but may also produce high proportions of discards and interact with vulnerable marine taxa. This study provides a comparative assessment of three métiers practiced in a Mediterranean SSF, each targeting a different species using static nets: gillnets for surmullet (Mullus surmuletus; MULLUS), and trammel nets for common cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis; SEPIA) and common sole (Solea solea; SOLE). A total of 334 hauls were analyzed between 2019 and 2023 under commercial fishing conditions. Catch composition was recorded at species level and categorized as target, retained bycatch, and discards, while elasmobranchs, predominantly comprising batoid species of varying conservation status, were treated as a separate category. Indicators describing catch characteristics and fishing practices included the proportions of immature and physically damaged individuals, catch-category biomass, fuel consumption standardized by landed commercial catch, soak time, fishing depth, haul income, and dolphin-depredation frequency. Principal component analysis and cumulative dominance curves were used to explore métier-specific patterns. The métiers differed in catch composition and in the profiles of ecological and operational indicators. MULLUS exhibited lower discard biomass shares and negligible recorded chondrichthyans biomass compared with two trammel-net métiers, but higher proportions of immature and damaged individuals and a higher frequency of dolphin depredation than SEPIA. SOLE had a high recorded contribution of elasmobranchs, while fuel-use intensity relative to landed commercial catch was highest in SEPIA. Hypothetical reclassification scenarios also illustrated how local market practices can affect estimates of retained bycatch and discards. The findings show that métiers operating in the same fishery can exhibit contrasting profiles, underscoring the need for métier-specific assessments and tailored management measures rather than assuming that interventions will be equally effective across fishing practices.
